Okie here.  The news at first acted like it was a 2015 type bitcoin lab in an abandoned home and then it turned out to be a commercial building with a faulty fire suppression system.  As a fire tech, I have no idea how no one noticed a leak of that magnitude since it would have flooded the building or blown out of the fire suppression drain line and both would have got someone’s attention quickly.  Odd.  If water usage outpaces the supply, mainline pressure falls and at a particular point below the pressure that the area choose, ground water can push or be sucked into a busted primary line.  Surface soil has tons of contamination and this results in a boil order that lasted about a week in this case.  Yukon and OKC have also had serious mainline bursts in the past week due to the heat which resulted in weeks long boil orders for tap water.  Im ready for fall yall, our infrastructure fails at 110° and -10° and that includes our HVAC units.

​Update Local Noise Ordinances: Pass strict municipal limits targeting low-frequency hums (C-weighted or Z-weighted sound levels) and continuous 24/7 noise, rather than standard daytime averages.
​Require Sound Mitigation Technology: Demand facilities install acoustic barriers, baffled ventilation, soundproof enclosures, low-noise cooling fans, or vibration isolators.

I live in Northern Virginia where we have the highest number of data centers in the country.  I write this long story in hopes one person reads it and learns the truth.  If it helps prevent another data center it will have been worth writing. Ten years ago we had only a few data centers, and they were mostly for the government and government services.  They blended into the landscape, like corporate buildings along a highway.  Then, like a tsunami wave, out of state companies showed up in droves.  Month after month they bought up natural land, pressured our local government - who were easily influenced - to rezone for commercial, and lobbied our officials to let them build massive data centers everywhere.  I mean, EVERYWHERE.  Turn your head and you’ll see one blocking out the sun and clouds, no trees or birds anymore, they’re all gone, replaced by towering walls of concrete for miles.  We can’t go anywhere without confronting soulless concrete monstrosities so ugly they make the brutalist movement look quaint. So heartwrenchingly imposing it feels stressful, traumatic, even dystopian to look at.  Entire forests and natural landscapes once protected by law were destroyed, overrun, and bulldozed.  Replaced by miles and miles of concrete with no aesthetic design or integration into the community.  They look like high security prisons encircling your neighborhood, your town center, your schools, entire stretches of road peppered with them one after another.  Think I’m exaggerating?  Come see for yourself.  Think I’m just some luddite?  I was a lawyer and lobbyist.  And not for who you think.

When it began happening many of us fought.  We were told the same tired lies—oh, it will create tax income, oh, it will create jobs, oh, it won’t have any environmental impact.  No one believed it—except our government who had accepted hundreds of thousands of dollars in campaign donations.  What happened?  Our remaining forests and farmlands—gone to overdevelopment! The energy suck of data centers is so IMMENSE that county residents are actually getting power outages on top of skyrocketing energy prices!  Taxes?  They actually got tax BREAKS as part of an economic development program.  Jobs?  Oh no.  Turns out the lifeless structures only need a small handful of rack monkeys to operate.  No real jobs were created unless you count the CEOs of the companies that own and built them.  In return, our soil and waterways are getting polluted.  The waste never disclosed by the owners must be dealt with, and the vast amount of water needed for these miles of machines is draining our drinking system.  Forget property values if they build next to your home/community, and they are.  

None of this is acknowledged by the absent T owners.  We are facing serious problems.  We have yet to hear a solution from a single executive or politician. Those of us old enough to remember the beauty of what used to be called horse and hunt country are heartbroken.  It didn’t need to be this way.  But greed is powerful.  Look closely at us.  Don’t ignore the lesson in our experience.  Fight these things with all your might.  You’ll be thankful you did.

Are Non-Disclosure Agreements Enforceable in Missouri?

Generally speaking, non-disclosure agreements are enforceable in Missouri as long as the agreements meet the requirements of a legally binding contract. There is no state law in Missouri that prohibits parties from creating non-disclosure agreements if the parties enter into the agreement voluntarily. However, an NDA can be deemed to be unenforceable if any of the following exists:

1) Ambiguous language. A non-disclosure agreement must contain specific and clear language to be considered enforceable and valid. If the language of the restrictive covenant is too broad or ambiguous, courts may invalidate the NDA.

2) Illegality. NDAs are not enforceable when the terms of the contract are against the law. If a party to the agreement can prove that the contract requires that party to do something illegal, the NDA will not be valid.

3) Lack of consideration. Like other contracts, non-disclosure agreements are valid only if there is "consideration", meaning compensation or payment. In other words, the parties must be motivated to enter into the agreement. If there is insufficient consideration, the court may invalidate the agreement altogether.

4) Unconscionable. A non-disclosure agreement is unconscionable when it contains provisions that are unjust to one of the parties.

5) Disclosures made before the NDA. If confidential information is disclosed before signing a non-disclosure agreement the contract is deemed unenforceable. The contract is unenforceable because the party receiving the confidential information did not agree to confidentiality at the time information was disclosed.

Data centres on the scale discussed require the output of entire power plants. With that much capacity now dedicated to servicing the Data Centre at much less revenue per kW, the utilities balance that by raising rates on everyone *else* in the area - especially since many utility companies are still local monopolies.
